summary: Presents functional requirements for deploying IP multicast within Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs, from both customer and provider viewpoints, to guide candidate solutions. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4834 lists what customer and provider networks need when a Layer 3 VPN carries multicast traffic. It guides solution designers but does not define a solution.

questions: ip multicast in provider provisioned vpn
what are the requirements for multicast in l3vpn
how does multicast work over a provider vpn
subtitle: Requirements for carrying customer multicast traffic across provider-run Layer 3 VPNs

tldr.problem: Existing Layer 3 provider VPNs did not natively support customer multicast, while simple tunnel workarounds could scale poorly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4834 lists customer and provider requirements for candidate multicast VPN solutions, including interoperability, scale, operations, and security.
tldr.outcome: The Informational RFC sets guidance for solution designers. It does not specify a multicast VPN protocol.

facts.label: Minimum customer IP MTU
facts.value: 1500 bytes, when the provider backbone allows

today: RFC 4834 is an Informational requirements document published in April 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC does not define a protocol.

sections.title: The Multicast VPN Problem
sections.content:
Customers may want to send one IP multicast stream to many sites connected through a provider-run Layer 3 virtual private network. The RFC says existing Layer 3 VPN solutions did not natively support this service.

Point-to-point tunnels can require provider-edge routers to copy traffic for many destinations, using bandwidth and router resources. RFC 4834 sets requirements for candidate solutions and applies to both IPv4 and IPv6, without choosing a design.
sections.plainLanguage: A company may need to send the same stream to many sites in its private network. This document describes what a suitable provider service should support.

sections.title: Use Cases and Expected Scale
sections.content:
The RFC discusses live broadcasts, many-to-many applications such as conferencing, data distribution, and VPN services that enable multicast by default. Its scale estimates draw on a survey with 13 responses collected in summer 2005.

The expected deployments range from one to several thousand multicast VPNs, with several hundred VPNs per provider-edge router and hundreds of streams per VPN or router. These are design expectations, not limits imposed by a protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples include broadcasts to many sites and conferences with many senders. A survey helped the authors describe the scale that future solutions might need to handle.

sections.title: Requirements from the Customer View
sections.content:
The service should be provisioned by the provider and should not require customer-edge devices to gain features beyond ordinary multicast support. The RFC requires support for PIM-SM, including source-specific multicast, and IGMPv3 for IPv4 and/or MLDv2 for IPv6.

Customers need multicast quality and availability comparable to unicast service, monitoring of traffic and resource use, and controls over which groups or channels are available. A multicast VPN must also support overlapping group addresses used by different customers.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers should be able to use multicast without replacing their edge equipment. The service should keep customers' traffic separate and provide ways to monitor its performance.

sections.title: Provider Scale and Resource Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Solutions must scale as the number of provider-edge routers, customer VPNs, sites, and multicast channels grows. The RFC also says a solution should let providers tune a trade-off between using bandwidth efficiently and limiting the forwarding state kept in the provider's core.

Following each customer's multicast tree can save bandwidth but requires more core state and quick updates. Aggregating streams can reduce state, but may send traffic to provider-edge routers that do not need it. Solutions should avoid dependence on a single tunnel technology and support inter-AS deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers must balance bandwidth use against the amount of routing information their network stores. A design that saves one resource may use more of the other.

sections.title: Operations, Interoperability, and Security
sections.content:
The requirements call for unicast and multicast to coexist in one VPN and for migration to have limited effect on existing service. Providers should be able to monitor traffic, resource use, and alarms, and diagnose how a customer's stream is carried through the network.

The RFC requires customer multicast security comparable to unicast VPN security. Traffic for a channel with no receivers in a VPN must not be propagated within that VPN. Inter-provider exchanges should support integrity and authenticity.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast should work alongside existing unicast service and be manageable by network operators. Traffic must stay within the VPNs that need it.
